content: 68W, pronounced as Six Eight Whiskey, is the Military Occupational Specialty (MOS) designation for healthcare specialists in the United States Army, commonly referred to as combat medics. These individuals are integral to the Army's operations, as every squad is required to have a combat medic present during hazardous missions. Their responsibilities span all stages of medical care in combat zones, from providing immediate treatment at the site of injury to maintaining care during evacuation and delivering medical services at healthcare facilities. Combat medics, particularly those at the entry level (68W10), are trained to operate in challenging and hazardous environments. They work closely with Army Physician Assistants (PAs) and doctors, performing a wide range of medical tasks. These tasks include administering immunizations, collecting fluid samples, obtaining vital signs, treating trauma, assisting in surgical procedures, and suturing wounds. In situations where medical professionals are unavailable, 68Ws are trained to provide Basic Life Support (BLS) and maintain patient stability. Senior 68Ws often take on leadership roles, such as serving as the senior enlisted personnel in clinical settings or as Platoon Sergeants in medical platoons. These roles involve additional responsibilities, including organizing training sessions, counseling soldiers, and overseeing the professional development of their teams. The 68W MOS is continually evolving to enhance the capabilities of these healthcare specialists. While the civilian equivalent of a 68W is an Emergency Medical Technician-Basic (EMT-B), additional training and education can lead to certifications or degrees in medical assisting or emergency medical sciences. Many 68Ws pursue further education to become Physician Assistants, Nurse Practitioners, Registered Nurses, Doctors, or Healthcare Administrators. The skill levels within the 68W MOS are tiered based on rank: Level 1: Entry-level combat medic (e.g., 68W10). Level 2: Combat medic at the rank of Sergeant (E-5). Level 3: Combat medic at the rank of Staff Sergeant (E-6). Level 4: Combat medic at the rank of Sergeant First Class (E-7). Level 5: Combat medic at the rank of Master Sergeant/First Sergeant (E-8) or Sergeant Major (E-9). Additionally, there are specific skill identifiers for specialized roles within the 68W MOS: F6: Army Flight Medic. M6: Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN). P6: Orthopedics Specialist. Y8: Immunization-Allergy Specialist. N3: Occupational Therapy Assistant. N9: Physical Therapy Technician. Y2: Identifier for those who have not completed upgrade training. W1: Special Operations Combat Medic (SOCM). P3: Optometry Specialist. Y6: Cardiovascular Specialist. The 68W MOS has undergone several changes over the years. Previously designated as 91W, the transition to 68W began in 2001 and was completed by 2007. During this period, medics were required to complete EMT-B certification, which had not been mandatory before. Those who failed to meet the new standards were reclassified into other MOSs. Training for 68Ws begins after basic training at Fort Sam Houston, where Advanced Individual Training (AIT) lasts between 16 and 68 weeks, depending on the specific skill identifier. This training covers a wide range of medical tasks necessary for their military careers. To maintain their MOS, 68Ws must keep their EMT and CPR certifications current, which requires ongoing training throughout their service. Advanced training opportunities are available based on the needs of their unit, such as learning advanced trauma treatments, administering medications, or using specialized hemorrhage control methods like Chitosan patches or QuikClot. Some 68Ws pursue further certifications, such as EMT-Intermediate (EMT-I) or EMT-Paramedic (EMT-P). The Army also offers the Interservice Physician Assistant Program (IPAP) for medics who wish to become Physician Assistants. A select few medics choose to become Special Forces Medical Sergeants (18D) or Special Operations Combat Medics (SOCM). SOCM-qualified 68Ws serve in elite units like the 75th Ranger Regiment, 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment, and Special Forces Groups. These medics operate with a high degree of independence, following specific protocols and providing advanced care in the absence of medical officers. The responsibilities of a 68W include providing cover fire during combat, accompanying patrols to deliver immediate medical care, stabilizing and triaging casualties, planning and conducting medical evacuations, and offering preventive and clinical care. They also play a crucial role in training non-medical soldiers as Combat Lifesavers (CLS). CLS-trained soldiers receive additional emergency medical training to provide point-of-injury care and act as a bridge between self-aid or buddy aid and the combat medic. This training includes skills such as casualty evaluation, airway management, controlling bleeding, managing chest injuries, and performing intravenous therapy. The CLS program aims to increase survivability in combat environments where a medic may not be immediately available.
